abstract: Student engagement is widely invoked as evidence of educational quality, yet its meanings are contested. This article examines how the concept is constructed and mobilised in UK higher education research, policy and institutional documentation. Drawing on Bacchi’s problematisation approach and Fairclough’s critical discourse analysis, it analyses a purposive corpus of 36 texts: 23 conceptual and research texts, two policy documents and 11 institutional documents from three West Midlands universities. Iterative close reading identifies three connected patterns. Multidimensional accounts of engagement are narrowed into visible proxies; evaluative infrastructures privilege meanings that can be documented and compared; and these constructions redistribute responsibility in ways that obscure unequal conditions of participation. Worked coding examples show how support, attendance, digital traces and regular logging become linked in institutional procedures. The article argues that recordable participation acquires authority because it can serve as evidence of both student conduct and institutional quality. This does not eliminate relational or participatory meanings, but places them at a disadvantage within systems organised around demonstrable performance. The contribution is to explain how the demand for evidence connects conceptual narrowing to unequal recognition, and why institutions should distinguish the visibility of participation from the conditions that make participation possible.

abstract: Intellectual activity is examined as a crucial component in the formation of dominant principles of perception, classification, and action. Drawing on Bourdieu’s field theory, the analysis focuses on the structural coincidence of struggles across relatively autonomous fields, showing how concordant principles may emerge without central coordination and contribute to naturalising the established order. Gramsci’s concepts of organicity, intellectual function, civil society, and common sense broaden this perspective by extending the range of agents, practices, and institutions implicated in hegemonic processes. This also foregrounds their relational and pedagogical dimensions and the need for an empirical inventory of the sites and symbolic forms through which common sense takes shape. Hegemony is thus treated as the contingent outcome of differentiated struggles whose effects become aligned across fields. A case study of agricultural capitalism in Romania illustrates the empirical operationalisation of this framework. For a fuller discussion and further developments of these themes: https://www.routledge.com/On-Gramsci-and-Bourdieu-Hegemony-Fields-and-Tools-for-Social-Research/Puoti-Roger/p/book/9781041299523

abstract: Forced displacement does not merely relocate people; it dismantles the material infrastructure through which place becomes memory. Drawing on 80 semi-structured interviews with Kurdish participants in their region of origin (n=25), Central Anatolia (n=25) and Western Europe (n=30), this article examines how the destruction, abandonment and transformation of inhabited space unmakes collective and intergenerational memory. Using Cernea's (1997) Impoverishment Risks and Reconstruction model alongside Malkki's (1992) critique of sedentarist assumptions about place, the analysis identifies four interlinked processes: urban redevelopment, rural demographic hollowing, diaspora gentrification, and the institutional foreclosure of access to common and sacred land. Participants describe memory as materially anchored, carried in streets, soil and threshold spaces, so that narrative transmission alone cannot repair its loss. The article argues that spatial memory loss is a distinct impoverishment risk inadequately addressed by existing frameworks, extends Cernea's model by specifying the memorial stakes of lost access to common property, and proposes the concept of inherited spatial memory: attachment to places the second generation has never physically inhabited.

abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic reignited longstanding debates around gender inequalities in paid and unpaid work. While survey research has advanced our understanding of these disparities, it typically relies on predefined categories and is susceptible to social desirability and recall bias. Online postings, by contrast, capture intimate experiences in real time but rarely include demographic attributes. We leverage a unique dataset of discussions in Reddit relationship communities that combines rich descriptions of conflicts around (un)paid work with demographic information to examine: Which topics do men and women discuss in relationship conflicts around paid and unpaid work? We use Large Language Models (LLMs) and systematically vary GPT-family models and prompting strategies to classify manifest (demographic information) and latent variables (whether posts discuss romantic relationships, paid, and unpaid work) in Reddit posts. Using classifications from the best-performing approach, we apply Structural Topic Models to explore which topics partners discuss and how discussions evolve over time. We find temporary pandemic shifts in topics, and women more often discuss mental health in paid work-related conflicts, while men more frequently emphasize career objectives. In conflicts related to unpaid work, men more frequently express concerns about sexual intimacy. Our analysis offers new insights into topics driving relationship conflicts around (un)paid work. We also contribute to the growing literature on LLMs’ capabilities and limitations in classifying social-science constructs. By combining demographic information with sensitive narratives, our dataset captures forms of relational conflict rarely accessible in survey or social-media research, opening promising avenues for future research.

abstract: The countries of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) are projected to see more than a threefold increase in dementia by 2050, due to a rapidly aging population. However, health care systems across Oman, Qatar, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia are still skewed towards acute rather than chronic care. Nurses are the primary dementia caregivers, but they often are not specialists. This situation is exacerbated by non-standardized curricula, heavy reliance on expatriate workforce, linguistic and cultural barriers, high workforce turnover, limited career incentives, and low public and institutional awareness, which delays diagnoses.This study synthesizes available regional and international evidence on dementia related nurse training and workforce preparedness in the GCC and develops evidence-informed policy recommendations for strengthening dementia education and workforce capacity. We propose several regional recommendations including accredited certification, compulsory continuing professional development, multidisciplinary care teams, and awareness-raising initiatives. Coordinated investment in specialized nurse training and workforce policy is important to prepare GCC healthcare systems for the region’s growing dementia burden.

abstract: Modern society increasingly prioritizes final products over the creative process, a trend exacerbated by the rapid adoption of generative AI. This study aims to explore the impact of AI integration into the creative process on subjective well-being and fulfillment, and to determine whether these effects differ between individuals creating for leisure versus those creating for a profession. Within this research, a quantitative-focused survey was conducted with 200 adults, categorized using a 2x2 design: acting as either a hobbyist or a professional illustrator, and either utilizing or not utilizing AI. The data reveals a consistent drop in a person’s well-being across both hobbyist and professional groups when AI is utilized. The differences in fulfillment between hobbyist and professional groups were not statistically significant. While a positive correlation was found between a product-focused mindset and satisfaction among professionals using AI, the overall satisfaction for AI users across the board remained significantly lower than for those who didn’t use AI. These findings suggest that AI integration into creative tasks carries measurable psychological costs by separating the creator from the intrinsically beneficial creative process, along with social costs that taint the creator-audience relationship. These findings underscore the value of human creation, suggesting that the ongoing conversation surrounding AI adoption must extend beyond efficiency to account for value within the human process. An avenue for further research lies within AI use in other fields less traditionally considered a “creative” discipline, such as STEM, which show evidence of having similar psychological benefits arising from the process.

abstract: Do larger polities hinder gender parity in elected office? We theorize that when populations grow faster than elected assemblies, a “seat congestion” effect intensifies competition for nominations, enabling men candidates to crowd out women. We test this argument using two nationwide natural experiments: Swedish municipal amalgamations in 1952 and 1973 that abruptly increased electorates. We track the effects in newly digitized historical panel data. Where electorate-per-seat ratios rose, growth in women's representation slowed. Decomposition analyses show that expanding councils only partially offsets congestion. By identifying polity size as a systematic brake on descriptive representation, the study adds a demographic dimension to debates on institutional design and points to an overlooked cost of increasing jurisdictional size.

abstract: Though the Supreme Court's 1954 decision in Brown v. Board of Education outlawed explicit segregation of public schools, segregation has remained stubbornly persistent in the intervening decades. What explains continuous racial segregation in the absence of explicit policy? One possible driver is America's built environment designed with similar segregationist impulses but not subject to the same corrective legal action. Zoning and land use policy influence where households of different means can live, thereby sorting their children across schools. We investigate this link drawing on housing unit counts from the American Community Survey, apportioned to 923 school district boundaries and 13,002 school attendance zones with 27 million residential parcels. We find that districts where single-family and multifamily housing is spread unevenly across attendance zones are more segregated by race and income. Schools with attendance zones that contain a higher proportion of single-family detached residences enroll a disproportionately high share of Asian and White students, as compared with their districts. When an attendance zone boundary is redrawn to encompass a higher share of single-family housing, its Asian and White share increases further. These findings help illuminate how land use policy influences educational segregation and contributes to literature on how policies that regulate the built environment affect racial sorting.

abstract: This paper examines how postdoctoral researchers navigate precarious employment conditions and claim career agency during an uncertain career stage. Drawing on a longitudinal qualitative interview panel of 35 postdocs from particle physics and modern history, the study distinguishes between two forms of agency: empowered strategizing and restricted drifting. Strategizing postdocs actively align short- to mid-term career goals with opportunities arising from fixed-term contracts and grant funding cycles, while drifting postdocs prioritize present research activities over long-term planning. Through in-depth interviews conducted in three waves, the analysis reveals how temporal horizons are compressed by the cyclical nature of academic recruitment and funding. The findings highlight the dynamic interplay between structural constraints and different forms of individual agency. This work contributes a processual perspective on career agency and precarity and adds to career research and studies of precarious working conditions.

abstract: This study examines how social networks are associated with unequal income returns to education and whether these associations vary by gender and across national contexts. Using data from the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP) 2017 from representative samples in 15 countries, the study analyses the interrelations between educational attainment, social ties, and personal income. The analyses distinguish both the status of social contacts and the type of ties to the upper middle class, while also examining variation by gender and country-level income inequality. The results show that access to upper-middle-class contacts is associated with wider educational differences in income, and that close ties, especially family members, relatives, and close friends, are more strongly associated with income than weaker ties. These patterns also vary by gender, with educated men’s income more strongly associated with upper-middle-class ties than educated women’s. In addition, educational differences in the association between social networks and income are more pronounced in countries with higher levels of income inequality. The study contributes to research on social stratification by showing that income returns to education are socially embedded and also vary by gender and national context.

abstract: This article proposes an evolutionary-materialist hypothesis on the origin of three basic patriarchal norms of reproductive behavior: restriction of divorce, control over female sexuality, and parental control over the choice of a spouse, which convergently emerge in societies transitioning to food production. These norms are viewed as an evolutionary adaptation to the conditions of the Neolithic transition, having emerged at the social level. Methodologically, the work is structured as a retrospective analysis of specific demographic conditions that created pressure in favor of such an adaptation. The starting mechanism is the reproductive strategy of "sex for resources"—the exchange of male- provided resources for female reproductive access—which arose in the ancestors of humans in the Paleolithic (or earlier) and was entrenched by sexual selection. Retrospective analysis shows that the most likely demographic challenges of the Neolithic transition, creating pressure in favor of the adaptation of reproductive behavioral strategies at the social level, were: (1) a manifold increase in population density, facilitating the switching of marital partners (primarily for men) and creating a threat of resource insecurity for women with children; (2) the emergence or intensification of awareness of the direct link between sexual intercourse and childbirth, which could reduce women's motivation for sexual activity due to awareness of reproductive costs; and (3) the dissociation between the timing of sexual and social maturation in males, as a result of which female hormonal mechanisms of partner choice (romantic love) continue to target young men who are not yet able to provide a family with sufficient resources under the new conditions. The convergent emergence of patriarchal norms of reproductive behavior in isolated cultures (Mesopotamia, China, the Aztecs, the Incas, and others) serves as evidence of their reproductive effectiveness compared to possible alternative adaptations. The hypothesis explains the specific role of older males (fathers) as the main agents maintaining these norms. The article is theoretical in nature and provides a foundation for further cross- cultural empirical research.

abstract: Immigrants who speak limited English earn less than those who speak it well. On the protective view of residential concentration, that differential should be smaller where immigrants are concentrated, because concentration supplies employers and customers who do not require English. On the isolation view it should be larger. This study tests both views in metropolitan Philadelphia, a former gateway whose immigrant population has grown again, with American Community Survey microdata for 2012 to 2024 and a two-level model of 7,355 foreign-born workers in 48 Public Use Microdata Areas. Hourly wages are about 8 percent lower per standard deviation of area immigrant density for foreign-born workers who speak English well and about 3 percent lower, an estimate not distinguishable from zero, for those who speak it poorly. Native-born workers in the same areas show a gradient of 2 percent, so most of the difference is specific to immigrants. The interaction between density and limited English is 0.049 (standard error 0.029) and disappears once occupation is held constant. The limited-English differential is 21 percent overall and 9 percent within an occupation, so most of it is associated with the occupations limited-English workers hold. An exploratory measure of the density of the worker’s own home language gives a positive interaction of 0.046 (0.022), driven by lower wages for proficient workers rather than higher wages for limited-English workers, and the same specification in the New York metropolitan area gives 0.045 (0.009). Higher earners move from the city to the suburbs.

abstract: The average lifespan has increased strongly in the past decades, but not everyone has benefited equally. Establishing the degree of intergenerational persistence of survival generates insights into broad inequalities between individuals and families in their likelihood to live to high ages. Using established register-type data for two regions in Northern and Southern Sweden 1880-2022 linked to historical records, we show that even before the rise of the modern social gradient in health in the 1960ies, mortality is lower among descendants from long-lived parents (top survivors of their birth cohort). This shared survival advantage between parents and children persists over time even after considering SES. Mortality among the descendants of top survivors is lower in lifestyle-related causes of death, suggesting that behavioral factors could be a significant factor in explaining the survival advantage. Overall, we find that mortality concentrates in families in patterns that go beyond the influence of SES alone. Similarities between relatives in health and mortality therefore provide an important lens into inequalities in survival and health over time.

abstract: Decomposition analysis is widely used to attribute changes in an aggregate outcome to changes in its underlying components. When several factors change simultaneously, however, sequential replacement generally yields different contributions depending on the order in which factors are replaced. The Shapley value resolves this problem by averaging marginal contributions over all possible orders, but the variation across those orders is itself potentially informative. This study proposes a decomposition method that analyzes this order dependence rather than averaging it away. For each factor, its contribution over all decomposition paths is treated as a function on the symmetric group. Harsanyi dividends are used to express path dependence in terms of interaction components, and irreducible representations of the symmetric group are then used to decompose the variance of path-specific contributions into interpretable spectral components. This framework distinguishes three properties of a decomposition result: average contribution, order instability, and the interaction complexity underlying that instability. For a decomposition with six factors, the method generates 64 counterfactual states and 720 replacement paths. Synthetic experiments confirm the predicted relationship between interaction order and admissible representation components and verify the numerical decomposition of order variance to machine precision. The empirical application examines fertility change among Korean women aged 20–49 using population size, age structure, marital composition, parity composition among married women, nonmarital fertility, and parity-specific marital fertility. Between 2000 and 2024, marital composition and parity-specific marital fertility contributed strongly to the decline in births, while changes in parity composition substantially offset that decline. The results also show that path-specific contributions can vary substantially around their Shapley means: for marital composition, parity composition and parity-specific marital fertility, the path standard deviation amounts to roughly 31–42% of the total change between 2000 and 2024. Cross-period differences in spectral structure, however, are strongly shaped by the magnitude of change over each interval. The proposed method extends decomposition analysis from the allocation of average contributions to the analysis of the full distribution and structure of path-specific contributions. It therefore provides an additional diagnostic layer for studying interaction, robustness, and structural dependence in multi-factor decomposition.

abstract: Prompt engineering has developed as a transformative subfield in artificial intelligence (AI), enabling humans to enhance AI systems through structured (PROLOG-like) instructions to perform specific tasks. This paper shines a light on its multi-dimensional impact on programming, routine tasks and broader AI applications, drawing on insights from recent studies. By using techniques such as parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), zero-shot learning, multi-shot learning and linguistic feature analysis, prompt engineering often is used to tackle remaining issues in software engineering (SE), language processing (NLP) and AI safety. The body of literature highlights its role in optimizing AI performance, reducing computational overhead and reducing biases. Additionally, it highlights critical gaps in current methodologies, such as the comparative energy intensity of state-of-art large language models (LLMs) and the requirements for adaptive and scalable prompt crafting strategies. Finally, the paper suggests future directions for research, highlighting the importance of human-centered design and collaboration to advance the field.

abstract: Cognition and culture have long been treated as parallel objects of study, joined more by metaphor than by mechanism. We argue they are co-constituted in a manner now empirically tractable: subjectivities can be measured as local trajectories through a high-dimensional cultural field, and the field is itself the aggregate of those trajectories. Recent advances in machine learning, including embedding methods and large generative models, provide the first general framework for measuring this co-constitution from micro-cognition to macro-social structure. Vector geometry recovers individual conceptual structure, organizational communication, and large-scale ideologies; captures multimodal cultural content beyond text; and generates testable predictions about cultural emergence, including the simultaneous arrival of independent discoveries across distant minds. We treat this predictability of simultaneous innovation as evidence for the co- constitutive view: when the geometry of the cultural field is measurable, trajectories of cognitive search through it become predictable. We then examine generative AI agents as simulators of human subjectivity and as a qualitatively new coordinating substrate whose insertion into social life introduces evolutionary dynamics unprecedented in human cultural history. We formalize this reflexive condition as a Heisenberg-like Uncertainty Principle for generative AI: as instruments for fixing a culture’s position grow more precise, our capacity to predict its trajectory degrades, because the machinery of cultural description and cultural action have merged. We close with ethical questions raised by AI-mediated cultural drift, recursive synthetic culture, and the limits of human cultural agency, offering guidelines for safe, equitable, and privacy-preserving research on AI and culture.

abstract: This article examines the historical development of Berberism in Algeria from the emergence of Algerian nationalist movements in the 1930s to the aftermath of the Black Spring of 2001. It argues that Berberism should not be understood as a stable political ideology with a fixed substantive meaning, but rather as a changing political practice through which the idea of a distinctive Berber identity has been mobilised in response to particular political contexts. The analysis distinguishes three phases in the development of Berber activism. The first, exemplified by the Berber Crisis of 1948–49, was largely an elite struggle within the Algerian nationalist movement over the definition of the Algerian nation and the recognition of its linguistic and cultural plurality. The second, crystallised in the Berber Spring of 1980, transformed Berberism into a broader social movement centred on cultural recognition, linguistic rights and opposition to state Arabisation. During the subsequent period of political liberalisation and civil war, Berber activism became increasingly institutionalised through political parties, social movements and transnational networks. The third phase, associated with the Black Spring of 2001, marked a significant reorientation. The declining legitimacy of established Berberist parties and the emergence of the Citizens’ Movement shifted political mobilisation toward territorial, socio-economic and increasingly Kabylia-centred claims. Drawing on concepts of political identity, recognition, nationalism and imagined communities, the article argues that this development contributed to the emergence of a specifically Kabyle nationalism. Whereas Berberism provided a broader cultural and transnational identity, it lacked a clearly defined territorial project capable of consolidating a common political community. The post-2001 mobilisation in Kabylia, by contrast, increasingly linked cultural identity to a specific homeland, territorial political structures and demands for autonomy. The article therefore conceptualises the transition from Berberism to Kabyle nationalism not as a linear transformation, but as a reconfiguration of political actors, strategies, territorial imaginaries and claims to collective self-determination. The article was written in 2012.

abstract: When does positive affect for a minority group translate into electoral protection for its rights? We examine this question for trans rights, which are being rolled back in many democracies. We ran a pre-registered experiment with 1,500 British adults in May 2025, weeks after the UK Supreme Court restricted the legal definition of `woman' to biological sex. Respondents chose between candidates from their preferred party who either endorsed or opposed the Supreme Court ruling, alongside other traits. We find a preference for candidates who endorse trans rights retrenchment that transcends much of the left-right divide. Crucially, although warm feelings toward trans people are twice as common as cold ones, cold affect translates more readily and more strongly into candidate choice. This asymmetry produces an overall electoral advantage for candidates endorsing trans rights retrenchment, with only those holding the warmest feelings toward trans people preferring candidates who oppose the ruling.

abstract: Observational studies of institutional decision-making often rely on explanatory variables that are themselves partly constructed through the process under investigation. In sentencing research, many legal factors are defined by the judge and may therefore act simultaneously as confounders and mediators. Controlling for them may introduce post-treatment bias, whereas omitting them may reintroduce confounding bias. We propose overcoming this impasse by conceptualising judicially-defined legal factors as variables affected by measurement error. Using a typical regression model of racial disparities in the U.S. Federal Courts, we demonstrate how sensitivity analyses based on SIMEX and Monte Carlo simulations can be used to assess the bias arising from judicial disagreement and judicial prejudice. We show that even modest levels of uncertainty in discretionary legal factors can generate substantial and unpredictable bias, affecting estimates of racial disparities even when measurement error is entirely random and therefore unrelated to race.

abstract: The mandate of the Philippines’ Commission on Higher Education ties faculty promotion in state universities and colleges to research publications. This commentary argues that the policy's emphasis on publication volume, unmatched by a corresponding verification mechanism, has created conditions in which predatory journals, conferences, and award bodies can thrive. Rising demand for indexed journal publications has already produced unsolicited offers to acquire legitimate, non-profit university journals, commercializing a system meant to signal quality. The threat extends beyond obviously fraudulent venues: recent evidence of paper mines (Barnett & Byrne, 2026), in which openly available datasets are mass-mined into formulaic, artificial-intelligence-assisted manuscripts that pass peer review in ostensibly legitimate journals, shows that volume-based incentives corrupt the research record even when every formal quality marker is present. Reading the Philippine case alongside this global pattern suggests that whitelisting indexed venues is necessary but insufficient. Accountability requires Philippine authorities to complement indexing criteria with a national research integrity framework, institutional verification of authorship, conference, and data provenance, and financial support that does not make ethical publishing contingent on personal wealth.

abstract: Abstract The paper explores the historical trajectory of Interhelpo, an industrial cooperative from Czechoslovakia, and its role in forging urbanization “from below” in early-Soviet town of Pishpek (now Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan). In light of scarce literature available on the success and failures of Western internationalist communes in the early Soviet period, this paper draws from intensive field work in Kyrgyzstan and understudied sources in Czech, Kyrgyz, Slovak and Russian to offer a novel, bottom-up narrative on the socialist city in Central Asia. Founded 1924 by Czech, Slovak, Hungarian, German internationalists and Ido-learners around the mountaineer and Bolshevik Rudolf Pavlovič Mareček in the Czechoslovakian town Žilina, the cooperative actively shaped urbanization in what would be become known as the capital of Soviet Kyrgyzstan. From 1925 until its liquidation during WWII, the cooperative built from scratch a whole district including the first electric power station of the city, textile and furniture factories, workshops for tailors, shoemakers and joiners, a school, a kindergarten, a tannery, a brewery as well as unique residential district. In the process, the cooperative forged an organic patchwork language referred to as spontánne esperanto to secure translocal collaboration between internationalists from Central Europe, on the one hand, and a heterogeneous mix of workers including Armenians, Kyrgyz, Dungans, Uygurs, Uzbeks, Russians and Ukrainians, on the other. Transcending a purely historical analysis, the paper ultimately turns to the urban landscape of present-day Bishkek. There it argues that while the district built by Interhelpo corresponds today to an exiled site dislocated by the hegemonic ethno-national memory regime, its materiality harbors relicts of another future capable of mobilizing alternative narratives on the city and her socialist and multi-ethnic past.

classification.note: Historical study of a Czechoslovak industrial cooperative building a district in early-Soviet Bishkek; weak link to enterprise formation.

abstract: Artificial intelligence is integrated into filmmaking and has attracted attention in human-computer interaction (HCI). Existing studies have primarily characterized AI systems for filmmaking by their capabilities and supported tasks, with limited attention to the organisation of filmmaking labor during system use. We review 31 HCI system papers and develop a three-layer taxonomy of labor sites, labor types, and human-AI allocation, examining where AI systems are positioned, what types of labor are involved during system use, and how those labor types are allocated between humans and AI. Our analysis reveals a concentration on individual below-the-line contexts, increasing attention to structural and meaning-making labor beyond execution, comparatively limited relational labor, and substantial variation in human-AI allocation across labor types. We further identify opportunities for the design and evaluation of AI systems that account for the broader organization of filmmaking labor. This review provides a labor-centered taxonomy for synthesizing AI systems for filmmaking and a basis for examining how AI may become involved in broader organizations of creative labor.

abstract: In global architectural literature, the mid-century high-modernist tower-and-slab block is widely pathologized as a failure of top-down social engineering. Anti-modernist critics routinely embrace architectural determinism, blaming concrete geometry for social decay. This paper challenges that consensus by examining Singapore, where high-modernist public housing constructed by the Housing & Development Board (HDB) shelters over 80 percent of citizens in safe, equity-building estates. Building on Katherine Bristol’s critique of the "Pruitt-Igoe myth," I demonstrate that building typology possesses marginal agency; the global demise of the high-rise slab resulted from welfare state retrenchment, fiscal starvation, and municipal abandonment. In Singapore, the typology succeeded due to a unique political-economic triad: radical land nationalization, captive domestic capital, and sovereign geographical enclosure. I adopt an object-oriented ontology and James Scott's notion of metis to argue the built form not as an empty vessel but being instrumental constructs that whose users will always develop new Métis and practical knowledges on how to maximise the utility of an urban form. I exemplify the Singaporean architects adapted the slab through vernacular inventions like the open-air "void deck." Ultimately, typology is not destiny but should be understood instrumentally.

abstract: Childhood cruelty to animals is among the most durable behavioral warning signs of later interpersonal violence in the forensic and clinical literature. The predictive mechanism does not rest on any settled answer about the moral status of the target. It rests on what the perpetrator practices, rehearses, and trains in themselves: desensitization, dominance affect, and the social learning of cruelty as pleasure. This paper offers a conceptual continuity argument and research agenda. We argue that the substrate of the target is incidental to that training, with one critical qualification: the configuration of the target matters. Routine digital destruction in static media (the static video game target, the scripted non player character) is a categorically different case from the closed loop, contingent emotional response systems on which the argument turns. As world models, embodied robotics, and closed loop emotional voice systems converge toward agents that perform distress in ways a user cannot reliably distinguish from a being in pain, we argue that the dispositional consequences of practiced cruelty against those agents are likely to recruit sufficiently similar mechanisms to warrant clinical and forensic attention. The paper does not claim that synthetic agents are moral patients. It claims that the warning signal forensic and clinical fields have relied upon for fifty years risks migrating to a venue with substantially diminished detection infrastructure. Existing human robot interaction research already shows that users do not need to believe a synthetic agent is conscious to respond to it through social, emotional, or dominance based scripts. The Kantian observation that cruelty corrupts the cruel is sufficient to ground the argument. Conduct disorder assessment, character evidence frameworks, school counseling protocols, and pre employment screening for sensitive roles will need to adapt or lose one of the more durable early behavioral indicators available to forensic and clinical assessment. The paper is offered as agenda setting; the operational protocols it identifies as necessary are deliberately scoped to a planned companion paper.

abstract: We introduce a novel measure of corporate hierarchy for 3,454 U.S. public firms. We construct this measure using online resumes of 18.1 million employees and a network estimation technique that allows us to identify hierarchical layers. Equipped with this measure, we document several facts about corporate hierarchies. Firms have on average six hierarchical layers and a pyramidal organizational structure. Firms with more layers have higher internal promotion rates and longer employee tenure. They exhibit higher operating performance and produce more patents, but not higher-quality patents. They also exhibit lower stock return volatility and operating asset volatility. At the same time, flatter firms fared better in response to the COVID-19 shock, consistent with greater organizational agility. We also examine potential determinants of hierarchical structures. Firms facing greater product market threats adopt flatter hierarchies. Moreover, firms increase their number of layers after going public, while they flatten their hierarchies following the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI). These findings are consistent with the theoretical predictions of existing models of corporate hierarchies and suggest that firms adjust their organizational structures to balance the benefits and costs of hierarchical layers.

abstract: This study examines how first-mover advantage was converted into durable elite dominance in seventeenth-century colonial Virginia, using this structural logic to critically evaluate twenty-first-century space resource law. Drawing on a Multilayered Frontier Capital Accumulation Model (MFCAM) that integrates frontier theory, world-systems theory, and institutional path dependence, the study addresses four research questions (RQ1–RQ4). Historical analysis shows how the First Families of Virginia (FFV), preempting land under the 1618 headright system, monopolized power through mutually reinforcing mechanisms of institutional pre-emption, marital closure, and symbolic capital accumulation, thereby converting land capital into political and cultural capital to maintain that dominance. At the same time, the study traces the formation of a lower-white stratum through indentured servitude, post-release landlessness, and racial divide-and-rule policies after Bacon's Rebellion (1676) and shows that elite and lower-class formation were two sides of the same institutional design. A comparison with the Massachusetts Bay Colony suggests these outcomes depended on early institutional choices. Based on these findings, the study conceptualizes a "Space Headright System" (SHS) comprising priority access to institutional design, revolving-door relations between regulators and industry, and the accumulation of legal precedent. By examining Section 402 of the 2015 U.S. Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act, the Artemis Accords, and national space resource laws, it assesses risks of lower-class formation such as space indentured servitude and space company towns. The study advances a conditional warning: if current legal trajectories continue, they suggest convergence toward a Virginia-type stratified order. To avert this, three policy recommendations (primary rules)—an international space cadastre, a Space Commons Fund, and treaty-based protections for later settlers—are proposed, alongside secondary design requirements to guard the implementing institutions against regulatory capture.

abstract: We measure how artificial intelligence (AI) affects the economy through its impact on software engineering productivity. We use information from financial markets to develop a forward-looking measure that is available in real time. We estimate the sensitivity of each firm’s stock return to an AI stock market index, and how this sensitivity depends on the share of firm payroll in software engineering. We use a model to map this cross-sectional relationship into software engineering productivity gains. From November 2022 to December 2025, AI increased the market’s expected present value of software engineering productivity by the equivalent of a permanent 32.6% productivity increase. The corresponding effect on the level of GDP is 3.6% in the baseline and 6.5% when higher software engineering productivity also raises R&D productivity. By mid-2026, amid rapid progress in coding agents, the effect of AI on productivity and GDP had more than doubled relative to the end of 2025. abstract: We study how business cycle fluctuations shape the pace and direction of innovation. Non-green innovation is procyclical, while green innovation is countercyclical, both over the cycle and in response to economic shocks. We explain this divergence in a dynamic general equilibrium model with endogenous green and non-green innovation. Green patents derive more value from distant profits, making green innovation less sensitive to short-run fluctuations. Endogenous innovation costs reinforce this mechanism, making green and non-green innovation effective substitutes. Evidence from market-implied patent valuations and scientist earnings supports the mechanism. The model implies larger and greener effects of innovation subsidies during downturns. abstract: We show that the dollar remains dominant in most aspects of global finance. The euro and renminbi are competing in an increasingly fragmented second tier of currencies, leaving no clear rivals to the dollar. We study how financial innovation could reshape the international monetary system. In principle, innovation levels the playing field between countries, for instance by reducing the need for vehicle currencies to intermediate transactions between other currency pairs and by making it easier to acquire and trade foreign assets. We show that an alternative outcome is more likely. Innovations that reduce frictions in cross-border transactions, especially dollar-backed payment stablecoins and other forms of tokenization of money, could interact with relative market thickness to reinforce the dollar’s dominance. This outcome is not preordained but depends on other countries’ willingness to embrace innovations and strengthen their financial markets and regulatory frameworks. While unipolarity has many disadvantages, we show that in some circumstances multipolarity might result in greater global fragility at times of financial market stress. abstract: This study examines a housing program that created affordable infill developments on formerly vacant, abandoned, or disinvested properties in Savannah, Georgia. Savannah is a major economic hub anchored by the Port of Savannah, where many urban neighborhoods remain impacted by disinvestment and climate risk. Using two decades of record-linked property and tax data, this study quantifies local economic spillovers from this public intervention, revealing previously hidden social and economic benefits of infill housing policies. These benefits include an 11% increase in the market value of properties immediately neighboring an infill development site and an increase of up to 35% in areas with a high density of infill activity, pointing to block-level revitalization in climate-disadvantaged and distressed areas. abstract: When does bad news stick?This paper shows that the persistence of media sentiment depends not only on whether news is good or bad, but also on what the news is about.Using the complete Wall Street Journal archive from 1990 to 2025, we construct monthly positive and negative sentiment indices for twelve economic topics and estimate topic-specific sentiment dynamics.Bad-news innovations generate larger cumulative responses than positive-sentiment innovations in every topic, indicating that negativity asymmetry is a broad feature of media sentiment.But the size of this asymmetry varies sharply across topics.The bad-minus-positive persistence gap is largest in security and human rights, firms and corporate strategy, health and public safety, and real estate and financial stability.Bad-news persistence is also sizable in data-rich topics such as financial markets, real estate, and corporate news, suggesting that frequent information arrival does not necessarily lead narratives to revert quickly.These findings show that aggregate sentiment indices mask substantial topic-level heterogeneity in the asymmetric dynamics of narratives, with potential implications for how persistent negative sentiment shapes expectations, asset prices, and real economic outcomes.

abstract: Whether imposing higher taxes on business owners adversely affects business activity by constraining investment and inducing capitalist flight is a central question in the ongoing debate on how to tax the ultra wealthy.To shed new light, I exploit a series of related Norwegian reforms during 2021-2024 that increased dividend tax rates, removed migration-related capital gains tax loopholes, and nearly doubled the effective marginal tax rate on business wealth.These reforms spurred international debate and, allegedly, an "exodus" of Norwegian billionaires (Financial Times, 2023).While I document clear effects on migration, these responses are concentrated among the top 0.1% of the wealth distribution and mostly confined to 2022 and 2023.My results indicate that at most 100 individuals left due to the reforms.I find no evidence of significant outmigration or reduced inflows of startup founders or inventors.I estimate that absent any outmigration, wealth tax revenues would have increased by 75%from 2021 to 2024.Reform-driven outmigration lowers the revenue gain to 71.5%.My findings further show that outmigrating owners' firms remain economically active and do not reduce investment.In a broader set of analyses, I examine whether business outcomes are affected, regardless of whether owners outmigrate, since firms may reduce investment both due to liquidity constraints or distortions to owners' savings decisions.I compare firms owned by Norwegian individuals subject to the wealth tax with firms owned by foreigners and other tax-exempt entities.By merging historical ownership data from Orbis with the Norwegian shareholder register, I perform these analyses on both Norwegian and foreign-domiciled firms.Across settings, I find no evidence that Norwegianowned firms pay out more dividends or invest less after the reforms, nor is there any evidence that the reform induced more bankruptcies.These findings indicate that the short-run economic costs of wealth taxation, in terms of migration and firm investment, are more limited than the public debate implies.

abstract: Frames not only shape societal debates but underpin the legitimacy of industries and institutions. Yet, even the most resonant frames can be turned on their head—weaponized against their initial intent. While framing research has studied competition between distinct frames, less is known about how a single frame’s meaning can be strategically inverted to serve opposing agendas. We conceptualize this process as “frame co-optation,” a potent but underexplored mechanism of discursive power that can alter institutional trajectories. The striking reversal of Germany’s nuclear energy phaseout provides a unique opportunity to examine frame co-optation. Using a multimethod machine-learning approach, we analyze three decades of the German nuclear energy debate to understand how the security frame, initially mobilized by antinuclear activists to justify a nuclear phaseout, was co-opted by pronuclear actors to advocate for its reversal. Our analysis shows how the pronuclear actors co-opted the security frame by perforating, camouflaging, infiltrating, and overwriting the frame’s meaning to invert its direction while preserving its resonance. We contribute to framing theory by introducing frame co-optation as a mechanism of strategic meaning inversion that can restore the legitimacy of controversial industries, and, more broadly, destabilize shared meaning and thereby amplify discursive polarization.

abstract: A growing volume of identity scholarship has started to challenge the Cartesian separation of body and mind, highlighting the importance of embodiment. While such research is enlightening, studies do not provide in-depth understanding of how some workers, but not others, are able to develop embodied identities (i.e., identities that are bonded with and bounded by their physical body). In particular, little is known about how this embodiment process occurs—or fails to do so—when changes within a worker’s body threaten their idealized identities (who they want and believe they should be). We examine this puzzle through an inductive study of perimenopause, which is a naturally occurring physiological transition experienced by most women. Unlike studies that have emphasized the importance of remedial identity or body work, our findings point to the criticality of an identity pause, which involves taking respite from striving to enact idealized identities. We illuminate how an identity pause gives workers the space to develop somatic attunement: the capacity to connect with, listen to, and respect their changing bodies. In so doing, our study calls attention to distinctive mechanisms that help develop embodied identities, advancing research on the body–identity nexus, embodiment, and women and work.

abstract: There has been recent and rapid growth in management and organizational research dedicated to the phenomenon of intergenerational transmission—the process through which organizations and other social systems reproduce and reconstitute themselves across long periods of time. This growth has resulted in several different research communities dedicated to understanding how organizational life transcends the involvement, tenure, and lifetimes of individuals. Yet, while assumptions about the nature of intergenerational transmission processes are coherent within research communities, such assumptions also diverge widely across such communities, resulting in contradictions and conceptual challenges. In this manuscript we identify four latent conceptualizations of the process of intergenerational transmission: taken-for-granted persistence, effortful maintenance, incremental adaptation, and discontinuous reinvention. We theorize that these processes represent different modes of what we term sociotemporal transcendence—different ways through which organizational life extends through time beyond the involvement or lifetimes of individuals. Based on these insights, we identify future research directions for a transcendence-based view of organizational life.

abstract: Despite a growing body of research on social marginalization in organizations, this scholarship remains fragmented across identity groups and disciplinary silos. As a result, organizational scholars lack a coherent framework to explain how marginalization persists and evolves across contexts. In this integrative review, we synthesize research from management, psychology, and sociology to develop a multilevel framework that conceptualizes marginalization as a recursive cycle between symbolic disadvantage (e.g., stereotyping, stigma, delegitimization) and material disadvantage (e.g., restricted access to jobs, resources, and institutional protections). We identify recurring mechanisms that operate across micro, meso, and macro levels, demonstrating how these dynamics mutually reinforce one another over time. Our framework also explains why interventions that target only one dimension of disadvantage often fall short or produce unintended consequences. We conclude by outlining a research agenda that advances theoretical development and empirical investigation of marginalization, including approaches to multilevel dynamics, temporal change, and measurement, as well as implications for designing more effective organizational interventions. Together, this integrative framework provides a unifying lens for understanding and addressing the cyclical dynamics of marginalization in organizations.

abstract: Awe has attracted substantial scholarly attention, but its implications for management remains fragmented across different accounts of what awe is and why it matters. In this review, we first show that the literature has developed around three dominant perspectives—collective self, epistemic, and well-being—each of which offers a distinct account of awe’s primary function. To integrate these perspectives, we advance a metamorphosis model of awe, which explains how awe first breaks down self- and nonself-schemata before building them back up again, producing an expansion of mind and self. We then organize the diverse elicitors of awe into cognitive, physical, social, and technological sources, clarifying the conditions under which awe is likely to arise. Through this model, we portray awe as a transformative emotion that influences identity, cognition, and behavior, with implications for core organizational processes such as leadership, work design, organizational change, sensemaking, and innovation. We conclude by charting a forward-looking research agenda calling for greater examination of awe’s role at the individual, team, and organizational levels.

abstract: While the geography of innovation is often studied at the level of city-regions, main conclusions provide only a partial account of the dynamics unfolding within cities. In this article, we examine how a set of proximate organizational sites located within a city comes to foster innovation. Specifically, we study how the placemaking practices of the entrepreneurs who originate these sites shape the localized landscape of resources that innovators mobilize to innovate. Drawing on the historical case of the Off-Off-Broadway theater (1958-1976), we show that these distributed, independent practices embedded an array of non-redundant resources within a small geographical area and, by fostering the patterning of innovators' attendance across proximate venues, cohered into an innovative micro-cluster. Our findings suggest that entrepreneurs who originate such organizational sites play an active role in infrastructuring innovation within cities, with implications for how we understand the spatial organization of innovation.

abstract: This study explores how Chilean university students perceive entrepreneurship, exploring whether they see it as an opportunity to address societal challenges or primarily as an enterprise creation. The research focuses on how these perceptions vary by gender in front of sociodemographic, academic, and institutional influential factors. Using a quantitative approach, we collected data from a sample of 973 students from different fields of study and conducted statistical analyses to determine the importance of factors that determine entrepreneurial attitudes. The results reveal that the majority of students see entrepreneurship as an opportunity to influence society and address social issues. Sociodemographic factors do not show statistical significance, suggesting that, within this specific population, they do not substantially alter the motivations for entrepreneurship. Although students may share similar views on the opportunity or business nature of entrepreneurship, the factors shaping this perception differ by gender. Among these factors, the value of active and engaged university support, especially in the form of experiential learning methodologies, in fostering opportunitydriven entrepreneurship is highlighted. In contrast, resources such as infrastructure and institutional culture, while important, appear to play a more limited role. This research underscores the need for a holistic approach to entrepreneurship education, but with special attention to particular differences between the segments being served, integrating institutional support with hands-on learning methods to better cultivate an entrepreneurial culture to economic growth and mindset geared towards addressing societal problems.

abstract: This paper examines M&A, representative changes, and business activity changes among Japanese firms in construction, manufacturing, retail, and agriculture using corporate data-based panel summaries and regression results. Firms with M&A experience are larger on average in the pooled descriptive data, but these differences are not exclusively pre-treatment comparisons. Descriptive Kaplan–Meier curves show no uniform M&A survival advantage: company-disappearance profiles differ in manufacturing and retail, while the displayed bankruptcy log-rank tests do not reject equality at the 5% level in any sector. Event-study regressions report cohort-specific coefficients for sales, employment, and customer counts in levels, with firm and year fixed effects and two-way clustered standard errors. The estimated trajectories vary across cohorts and outcomes, and some pre-event differences call for caution in causal interpretation. Conditional Cox models associate M&A with lower exit hazards across all four sectors. The separate counterparty turnover analysis demonstrates qualitative network upgrading rather than mere link-count contraction: in construction, newly added customers exhibit significantly higher capital scale and sales than discontinued partners. Pair regressions identify sector-specific distance and capital associations, and the executive-age analysis finds an M&A-probability discontinuity at absolute age 70 in retail, which disappears when centered around industry retirement peaks. These results distinguish conditional hazards and counterparty restructuring from unadjusted survival comparisons and gross customer counts.

abstract: We examine the long-term relationship between historical levels of self-employment and economic performance in different regions of Germany. A particular distinction is made between West Germany and the eastern part of the country, that came after WWII for forty years under socialist regime. Regional self-employment rates exhibit high correlation over time periods exceeding a century. In West Germany, high and increasing levels of self-employment are significantly associated with high current levels of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) per population, despite several major historical shocks. That such a relationship cannot be found in East Germany could be a legacy of the socialist period where the government performed anti-entrepreneurial policies. We also find a positive relationship between historical self-employment and patenting in both parts of the country. This relationship is, however, somewhat weaker in East Germany, which experienced considerably more historical shocks than West Germany.

abstract: This study examines the dynamics of regional innovation activity in Europe from 2000 to 2020 using patent applications. Standard convergence measures indicate that regional disparities are narrowing, with initially lagging regions catching up to the leading ones. Our analysis reveals two persistent â€˜clubsâ€™: the â€˜laggingâ€™ and the â€˜advancedâ€™ regions. Although these groups are becoming increasingly similar, the differences between them remain largely unchanged. Despite two decades of growth, the disparity between the two clubs still accounts for a great deal of the total variation in regional patenting. These patterns suggest a convergence illusion that is overlooked in the current scholarly debate.

abstract: Remittances and social protection programmes have become two of the most important sources of financial support for households across low- and middle-income countries. While both have been linked to household investment and livelihood diversification, little is known about how they jointly influence entrepreneurship. This paper examines whether public transfers, in the form of cash transfers and school feeding support, crowd out or in household entrepreneurship and whether private transfers, in the form of remittances, complement or substitute for public transfers in shaping entrepreneurship. Using household survey data from eight communities in West Africa, we analyse the relationship between social protection, remittances and a range of entrepreneurial outcomes. The results provide little evidence that social protection systematically influences household entrepreneurship or alters the relationship between remittances and business activity. In contrast, remittances remain consistently associated with business creation and entrepreneurial intentions across multiple contexts. These findings suggest that expanding social protection does not diminish the productive role of remittances and highlight the importance of considering public and private sources of household support jointly when assessing policies aimed at promoting entrepreneurship and inclusive economic development.
